BAHA'I - THE WAY TO UNITY AND PEACE

OPENING QUOTES
- From the Writings of Baha'u'llah (LXXVI): "Every created thing in the whole universe is but a door leading into his knowledge, a sign of his sovereignty, a revelation of his names, a symbol of his majesty, a token of his power, a means of admittance into his straight path."
- The same passage says creation is so perfect that no mind or heart can ever grasp the nature of even the smallest creature, much less the mystery of God, "the day star of truth", "the invisible and unknowable essence".
- Main idea: all creation points to God, but God himself is beyond full human understanding.
- Abdul Baha (eldest son of Baha'u'llah): "To be a Baha'i simply means to love all the world; to love humanity and try to serve it; to work for universal peace and universal brotherhood."
- Main idea: Baha'i is about love of all humanity, service, universal peace and brotherhood.

KEY TERMS (ONE-LINE DEFINITIONS)
- Imam or Bab: "Bab" means "gate"; Ali Muhammad claimed to be the twelfth Imam or Bab, the gate through whom God communicated with humanity.
- Baha'u'llah: means "Glory of God"; the title taken by Mizra-Husayn-Ali, founder of the Baha'i faith.
- Abdul Baha: means "Servant of Baha" or "Servant of Glory"; title of Baha'u'llah's eldest son and successor.
- Shoghi Effendi (The Guardian): grandson of Abdul Baha, leader from 1921 to 1957.
- House of Justice (Universal House of Justice): the supreme legislative body governing international Baha'i administration.
- Spiritual Assembly: the basic local unit of Baha'i organisation, nine or more adults, representatives elected every year.
- National Assembly: the second level, also with nine delegates elected every year.
- Ridvan: "Lord of Feasts", the most important Baha'i festival (21 April - 2 May).
- House of worship: a nine-sided Baha'i temple, a place of quiet contemplation with no ceremonies.
- Pioneers: volunteers who do all the work of teaching and spreading the faith.
- The Book of the Covenant: the book in which Baha'u'llah interpreted his revelations.
- Kitab-I-Aqdas: the "Most Holy Book", dealing with laws and institutions.
- Kitab-I-Iqan: the "Book of Certitude", about God's revelations to humankind.
- Apostate: a deserter of a religion; Baha'is are attacked as apostates from Islam.

ORIGINS: THE BAB (ALI MUHAMMAD)
- The Baha'i religion began in Iran in 1844.
- It springs from Islam.
- Ali Muhammad, a Persian Shiite Muslim, declared he was the twelfth Imam or Bab (gate), through whom God communicated with humanity.
- He was the long-awaited spiritual leader through whom believers would have access to the true faith.
- He launched a movement of spiritual and social reform.
- This was to prepare for the soon-to-come appearance of a divine leader who would bring all humanity to universal peace.
- His group was seen as such a threat that he was executed in 1850 by angry and fearful religious and political forces.
- He kept his followers' hope alive by announcing a greater leader to come.

BAHA'U'LLAH (GLORY OF GOD)
- Among the Bab's followers was Mizra-Husayn-Ali, who took the title Baha'u'llah (Glory of God).
- He began to preach and gathered a large community of followers.
- 1863: at an assembly of his followers in Baghdad he claimed to be the promised divine leader. All who recognised him as the Chosen One of God were to follow him.
- He announced his mission: to promote the unity of humankind and establish a true, universal religion.
- He spent many years in exile (a passport was issued to him and his family when exiled from Persia) but kept guiding his followers, especially through his writings.
- He died in Israel in 1892. As he had requested, his eldest son took over the leadership.

ABDUL BAHA AND SHOGHI EFFENDI
- Baha'u'llah's son took the name Abdul Baha (Servant of Baha / Servant of Glory).
- He preached throughout Europe, Canada and the United States and set up many communities worldwide.
- He was the authorised interpreter of the Baha'i faith.
- He died in 1921. His will directed his grandson to continue as leader.
- Shoghi Effendi (The Guardian) led until his death in 1957, promoting the unification of humanity through Baha'i teachings.
- He established the House of Justice, the supreme legislative body governing international Baha'i administration.

ORGANISATION
- Basic unit: the local Spiritual Assembly - nine or more adults, with representatives elected annually.
- Second level: the National Assembly - nine delegates elected annually.
- Top level: the (Universal) House of Justice.
- Baha'i institutions are social, not ecclesiastical (church-like) or hierarchical.

THE TEACHINGS OF BAHA'I
- Key aims: the ONENESS OF GOD and the UNITY OF HUMANITY.
- God has made his truth known through prophets and divine teachers in every era: Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Krishna, Buddha, Christ, Muhammad and Baha'u'llah.
- Each prophet suited the stage of development of humankind at that time.
- Different religions grew from people's interpretations of these prophets' messages.
- Baha'u'llah saw himself as renewing the world and fulfilling the promises of all religions.
- He came to clear away the errors and misunderstandings of former religions and to speak God's message of truth anew.
- This will not bring an immediate restoration of moral values and community wellbeing, but an INNER CHANGE in each person, leading to world peace and harmony.
- Baha'is believe Baha'u'llah came to rescue the world from moral, social and spiritual disintegration and fill it with justice and peace through a new world order.

THE TWELVE TEACHINGS (SUMMARISED BY ABDUL BAHA)
- 1 Humanity, 2 Truth, 3 Religions, 4 Science, 5 Sex, 6 Prejudice, 7 Peace, 8 Education, 9 Economy, 10 Human Rights, 11 Language, 12 Work.

JUDGEMENT AND AFTERLIFE
- The Day of Judgement is a current, daily test (not only a future event).
- After death, each person's soul is made up of the moral and spiritual qualities developed during their physical life.
- Heaven and hell are conditions of the soul, not places.
- Heaven = true harmony with God. Hell = the absence of this harmony.
- Baha'is believe in a God who reveals himself to humankind and offers the promise of an afterlife - common ground with other monotheistic faiths for dialogue.

THE LIFESTYLE OF BELIEVERS: WORSHIP
- Baha'is meet in members' homes for prayer.
- Religious services are a spiritual preparation for the social task of active community service and promoting the Baha'i cause.
- No set rituals for worship and no priests.
- Worship = prayer and spiritual reading.
- Daily work is also an act of worship when done in a spirit of service to God and the human family.

FESTIVALS
- Festivals are based mainly on important historical events and anniversaries, for example the birth of Baha'u'llah on 12 November.
- RIDVAN ("Lord of Feasts") is the most important festival. It lasts twelve days, 21 April to 2 May. It commemorates Baha'u'llah's declaration of his mission in the Ridvan garden outside Baghdad.

HOUSES OF WORSHIP
- No ceremonies take place in houses of worship (temples); they are places of quiet contemplation.
- Every house of worship has NINE sides. Nine, the largest single digit, symbolises oneness and unity.
- They are set in large gardens with fountains and trees. The surrounding buildings are used for education and social purposes.
- Example pictured: the Baha'i Lotus Temple, Delhi.

OBLIGATIONS AND MORAL RULES
- Teaching and spreading the faith is done entirely by volunteers called pioneers.
- Obligations: daily prayer; nineteen days of fasting through the month of 'Ala'; education of children.
- Baha'is do not drink alcohol, take drugs, gamble or gossip.
- Marriage is a lifelong commitment.

BECOMING A MEMBER
- Apply to the local Spiritual Assembly.
- Accept the tenets (beliefs) of the faith.
- Recognise the prophethood of the Bab, Baha'u'llah, Abdul Baha, Shoghi Effendi and the Universal House of Justice.
- Accept the scriptures of these prophets, especially:
- the Kitab-I-Aqdas (Most Holy Book) - laws and institutions;
- the Kitab-I-Iqan (Book of Certitude) - God's revelations to humankind.
- Baha'u'llah interpreted his revelations in "The Book of the Covenant".
- He appointed his oldest son as the only authority allowed to interpret his revelations; the son in turn appointed the eldest grandson.
- Since the grandson's death in 1957, no individual can claim this authority.
- Many Baha'is are converts and are mostly committed and active in their faith.

NUMBERS AND WHERE BAHA'IS LIVE
- Fact box: about six and a half million followers worldwide; one and three quarter million in India; three quarters of a million in the USA; a quarter of a million in Bolivia; also followers in Chad and Zambia in Africa.
- "Baha'i Faith Today" section: some seven million adherents in over 70,000 centres worldwide; almost two million in India; three quarters of a million in the USA; smaller communities in Europe and Africa. (Note: the chapter gives slightly different totals in the two places.)

THE BAHA'I FAITH TODAY
- Baha'i claims to be a wholly independent, revealed religion.
- International headquarters: Haifa, Israel, where the shrine of the Bab is on Mount Carmel.
- IRELAND: the faith began here in 1918 when George Townsend, sometime canon of St Patrick's Cathedral, Dublin, became a Baha'i.
- There are over forty Baha'i communities in Ireland today.

PERSECUTION AND CONFLICT
- From the start Baha'is have been persecuted in the Middle East and attacked as apostates (deserters) from Islam.
- This hatred is especially strong in Iran, where official oppression has reached "unbearable proportions".
- Examples in Iran: Baha'i schools closed; Baha'i marriages declared invalid; birth certificates refused; Baha'i cemeteries violated; buildings destroyed.
- These human rights abuses continue today despite protests by the international Baha'i community.
- The Baha'i message could be seen as a threat: e.g. claiming a prophet after Muhammad, and claiming to fulfil all religions.

CHAPTER KEY TERMS LIST
- Imam or Bab, Baha'u'llah, House of Justice, Spiritual Assembly, Ridvan, House of worship, The Book of the Covenant.

rows.model_answer: Baha'u'llah led the faith until his death in Israel in 1892. His eldest son, Abdul Baha, then led and preached in Europe, Canada and the USA until 1921. His will made his grandson Shoghi Effendi (The Guardian) leader until 1957; he set up the House of Justice.

rows.prompt: Name four of the twelve Baha'i teachings summarised by Abdul Baha.
rows.model_answer: Any four of: Humanity, Truth, Religions, Science, Sex, Prejudice, Peace, Education, Economy, Human Rights, Language, Work. For example: Peace, Education, Human Rights and Prejudice.

rows.prompt: Outline the origins and early development of the Baha'i faith.
rows.model_answer: The Baha'i religion began in Iran in 1844 and springs from Islam. Ali Muhammad, a Persian Shiite Muslim, declared that he was the twelfth Imam or Bab (gate) through whom God communicated with humanity. He launched a movement of spiritual and social reform to prepare for the coming of a divine leader who would bring all humanity to universal peace. His group was seen as a threat and he was executed in 1850, but he kept his followers' hope alive by announcing a greater leader to come. One follower, Mizra-Husayn-Ali, took the title Baha'u'llah (Glory of God) and gathered a large community. In 1863, at an assembly in Baghdad, he claimed to be the promised divine leader. His mission was to promote the unity of humankind and establish a true, universal religion. He spent many years in exile, guiding followers through his writings, and died in Israel in 1892. His eldest son, Abdul Baha (Servant of Glory), preached in Europe, Canada and the USA and founded many communities. In 1921 leadership passed to his grandson Shoghi Effendi (The Guardian), who led until 1957 and established the House of Justice, the supreme legislative body of the faith.

May refer to: Iran 1844; roots in Islam; Ali Muhammad as Bab/twelfth Imam; reform movement preparing for a divine leader; execution 1850; Baha'u'llah (Glory of God); Baghdad 1863 claim; mission of unity and universal religion; exile and writings; death in Israel 1892; Abdul Baha's preaching; Shoghi Effendi 1921-1957; House of Justice; Spiritual Assemblies.

rows.prompt: 'To be a Baha'i simply means to love all the world.' Discuss how the teachings of the Baha'i faith reflect this vision of unity.
rows.model_answer: Abdul Baha said that being a Baha'i means loving all the world, serving humanity and working for universal peace and brotherhood. Baha'i teaching reflects this in many ways. Its key aims are the oneness of God and the unity of humanity. Baha'is believe God revealed his truth through prophets in every era, including Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Krishna, Buddha, Christ, Muhammad and Baha'u'llah, each suited to humanity's stage of development. So all religions are seen as connected, and Baha'u'llah came to clear away misunderstandings and fulfil the promises of all religions. Abdul Baha's twelve teachings include Humanity, Peace, Prejudice, Human Rights, Education and Language, all of which aim to break down barriers between peoples. Baha'is believe peace will come not by force but through an inner change in each person. Daily work done in a spirit of service to God and the human family counts as worship, and religious services prepare members for active community service. Even the nine-sided houses of worship symbolise oneness and unity. However, the vision has not been returned by all: Baha'is are persecuted in Iran as apostates from Islam.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: meaning of the quote; oneness of God and unity of humanity; series of prophets; religions as interpretations; Baha'u'llah fulfilling all religions; twelve teachings (esp. peace, prejudice, human rights, language, education); inner change; work as worship and service; nine-sided temples; independent of race/nation. Must discuss the statement, linking teachings to unity.

rows.prompt: Describe the worship and lifestyle of members of the Baha'i faith.
rows.model_answer: Baha'i institutions are social rather than church-like or hierarchical. Baha'is meet in members' homes for prayer, and these services prepare them spiritually for active community service. There are no set rituals and no priests; worship consists of prayer and spiritual reading, and daily work is also worship when done in a spirit of service to God and the human family. Festivals mark historical events, such as the birth of Baha'u'llah on 12 November. The most important is Ridvan, the Lord of Feasts, held over twelve days from 21 April to 2 May, recalling Baha'u'llah's declaration of his mission in the Ridvan garden outside Baghdad. Houses of worship have nine sides, symbolising oneness, and are places of quiet contemplation where no ceremonies take place. Baha'is pray daily, fast for nineteen days during the month of 'Ala' and educate their children. They do not drink alcohol, take drugs, gamble or gossip, and marriage is a lifelong commitment. Volunteers called pioneers spread the faith.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: home prayer; no priests or set ritual; prayer and spiritual reading; work as worship; festivals incl. 12 November and Ridvan (dates, meaning); nine-sided houses of worship, contemplation; daily prayer; 19-day fast in 'Ala'; education of children; no alcohol, drugs, gambling, gossip; lifelong marriage; pioneers; joining via Spiritual Assembly.

rows.prompt: Outline two ways in which members of the Baha'i faith have experienced persecution.
rows.model_answer: From their earliest days, Baha'is have been persecuted in the Middle East and attacked as apostates (deserters) from Islam. The founder of the movement, the Bab (Ali Muhammad), was executed in 1850 by outraged and fearful religious and political forces, because his new group was seen as a threat. His follower Baha'u'llah also spent many years in exile from Persia, and a passport was issued to him and his family at that time, although he continued to guide his community through his writings. Part of the reason for this hostility is that the Baha'i message, which claims a new prophet after Muhammad and claims to fulfil all religions, could be perceived as a threat by orthodox Islam. Today persecution is especially severe in Iran, where official oppression has reached unbearable proportions. Baha'i schools have been closed, Baha'i marriages declared invalid, birth certificates refused, cemeteries violated and buildings destroyed. These abuses of human rights continue despite the protests of the international Baha'i community.
